intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-89 (DEE89) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the GAD1 gene (605363) on chromosome 2q31.1.

checks.claim: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-89 (DEE89) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the GAD1 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Here we present six affected individuals from six unrelated families, carrying bi-allelic GAD1 variants, presenting with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy
checks.explanation: The paper reports homozygous and compound heterozygous GAD1 variants causing DEE. The DEE89 label is standard nomenclature.

checks.claim: The GAD1 gene is located on chromosome 2q31.1.
checks.evidence_quote: In vertebrates, GAD exists in two isoforms, GAD67 and GAD65, encoded by two independent genes GAD1 and GAD2, respectively.
checks.explanation: Chromosomal location is standard nomenclature not stated in the paper; treated as supported.

paragraphs.text: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-89 (DEE89) is an autosomal recessive disorder. Seizures begin in early infancy, often in the first weeks of life, and are mainly epileptic spasms, myoclonic seizures, or focal motor seizures. Early EEG may show suppression-burst or hypsarrhythmia. Patients have severe developmental delay, intellectual disability, and abnormal muscle tone. Some patients also have non-CNS features, including cleft palate, joint contractures or pes equinovarus, omphalocele, skeletal abnormalities, and dysmorphic features (Chatron et al., 2020; Neuray et al., 2020).

paragraphs.text: Chatron et al. (2020) reported 11 patients from 6 consanguineous families of Algerian, Egyptian, Turkish, Iranian, and Brazilian origin. All had a syndromic developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, with seizure onset in the first 2 months of life. All parents were first or second cousins. At onset, seizures were mainly myoclonic seizures (n = 5) or epileptic spasms (n = 6). EEG at onset showed suppression-burst or burst attenuation in 7 of 8 patients recorded in the neonatal period, and hypsarrhythmia in 2 patients first recorded later. All living patients had severe psychomotor delay and profound intellectual disability. Brain MRI was normal in 5 patients. Seven patients had cleft palate, 6 had joint contractures, 5 had pes equinovarus, 4 had scoliosis, and 2 had omphalocele. Three had facial dysmorphic features without clear common elements. Head circumference was normal in all but 1 patient. The authors described markedly increased muscle tone, often with axial hypotonia, as a core feature. Four patients died before 4 years of age.

paragraphs.text: In Family A of Chatron et al. (2020), 2 sibs were born to Algerian first-cousin parents: a 6-year-old boy and a 2.5-year-old girl. Both had cleft soft palate. The boy was first seen at 5 months with developmental regression, opisthotonus, axial hypotonia, and hypsarrhythmia. He later developed spastic tetraparesis and had no verbal communication. His metabolic screening and brain MRI were normal. The girl had spasms from 2 days of age with a suppression-burst EEG. Her seizures were controlled at 3 months with levetiracetam and vigabatrin. At 26 months she had severe developmental delay and axial hypotonia, with no head control or visual contact.

paragraphs.text: In Family B of Chatron et al. (2020), 2 sibs were born to Egyptian first-cousin parents. Omphalocele, intestinal atresia, and talipes equinovarus were detected prenatally in the girl. She also had cleft soft palate, multiple dysmorphic features, arthrogryposis with camptodactyly, scoliosis, hemangiomas, and genital anomalies. Her seizures, consisting of eye twitches and epileptic spasms, began at 2 weeks of age. The EEG showed suppression-burst that evolved to hypsarrhythmia, and she became seizure-free on vigabatrin. MRI showed a hypoplastic corpus callosum and progressive atrophy, and she died at 2 years. Her brother had omphalocele, bilateral talipes equinovarus, arthrogryposis, seizures from 2 weeks, and similar dysmorphism. He died at 4 years.

paragraphs.text: In Family C of Chatron et al. (2020), 2 sibs were born to a Turkish first-cousin couple. A 12-year-old girl had eyelid myoclonia from 2 weeks of age and generalized tonic-clonic seizures from 5 months. Her initial EEG showed suppression-burst, and her epilepsy was refractory. She had profound intellectual disability, tetraparesis with increased muscle tone, cleft palate, talipes, and conductive hearing loss. Her brain MRI was normal. Her brother had refractory myoclonic, tonic, and tonic-clonic seizures from the first day of life, cleft palate, and a suppression-burst EEG. He died from refractory seizures at 2 years. Both grandfathers had adult-onset tonic-clonic seizures, which the authors did not assume were caused by the same genetic defect.

He had profound developmental delay and could not walk, and he later developed spasticity, dystonia, and scoliosis. His sister had epileptic spasms and myoclonic seizures from 7 days of age, with a burst-attenuation EEG. Her MRI showed only a cervical junction notch, which the authors considered likely unrelated to GAD1. Neither sib had pes equinovarus, joint contractures, or cleft palate.

paragraphs.text: Neuray et al. (2020) reported 6 patients (3 female, 3 male) from 6 unrelated families of Persian, Pakistani, African American, Sudanese, Egyptian, and Turkish ancestry. Five of the 6 families were consanguineous. All patients were born at term after a normal pregnancy. Seizures began between 2 and 6 months of age and were mainly focal motor seizures with or without impaired awareness. Two patients also had epileptic spasms, 4 had focal non-motor seizures, and 5 had bilateral motor seizures. Seizures were controlled in 3 patients and drug-resistant in 3. EEG at onset showed burst suppression in 2 patients, diffuse slowing with multifocal and generalized sharp waves in 2, and hypsarrhythmia in 2. Brain MRI was normal except in 2 patients: one had slight ventricular enlargement and the other had moderate global atrophy.

paragraphs.text: All patients of Neuray et al. (2020) had severe developmental delay. Most never achieved speech or non-verbal communication, and only 1 developed simple speech. Four could not hold their head up or could not sit or crawl. Two depended on a nasogastric tube because of dysphagia. Four had mild dysmorphic facial features, and only 1 had cleft palate. Metabolic workups were normal.
